petrous

PEH-truss · adjective

What It Means

Petrous is resembling stone in hardness or density.

The archaeologist noted that the fossil's petrous core had resisted millions of years of erosion while softer material around it crumbled away.

Example

Surgeons often need a special drill to reach the petrous portion of the skull, since the bone there is unusually dense.

Bone so dense it requires a specialized drill is exactly the stone-like hardness petrous describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

stony: Stony means having the hardness or feel of stone, and it slides easily into feeling -- a stony stare, a stony silence. Petrous stays literal and technical: it describes actual material, like bone or fossil, that has taken on stone's hardness and density.

rocklike: Rocklike is the everyday, informal comparison -- anything that strikes you as solid as a rock. Petrous names the same stone-like hardness but is the formal, technical term, the one a surgeon or geologist reaches for when describing dense bone or mineral.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

spongy: soft and easily compressed

Where it sits · how hard and unyielding it is

firm → petrous → adamantine

firm vs. petrous: Firm simply means solid enough to resist light pressure -- an everyday, moderate description; petrous specifically evokes the hardness of actual stone.

adamantine vs. petrous: Adamantine pushes hardness to an almost mythical, unbreakable extreme, while petrous stays grounded in the literal comparison to stone or rock.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — petr: rock, stone (Greek/Latin (petra))

suffix — -ous: possessing the quality of (Latin)

Put it together: Petrous comes from Greek/Latin petra ('rock, stone') + -ous ('possessing the quality of') -- literally 'possessing the quality of stone.'

Use the root in a new word: petrify: The gift shop sold polished slices of petrified wood next to the postcards.

Word Choice

Petrous is mostly a technical, anatomical or geological term (the petrous bone protects the inner ear), though it can describe any material or structure that has taken on a stone-like hardness or density.
